utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is being brought in if I could just alert the Trial Chamber to one administrative matter, as it were. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that it shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, please sit down. As it is not the first time that you are giving evidence here in the Tribunal, you know the procedure. Mr. Thayer has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying in this building almost four years ago in October of 2006?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recently read all of your testimony in that case, the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you attest before this Trial Chamber that what you read accurately reflects what you said during that trial?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That matched exactly what I said, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you further attest that, were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in October of 2006, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct because there's just one story.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P597 and P598, Colonel Franken's Popovic testimony, the former being under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Given the extensive nature of Colonel Franken's prior testimony, I have a 92 ter summary that may take a couple of minutes, so please sit back and I'll have about three and a half pages to read. I've tried to reduce it, but Colonel Franken's level of knowledge and participation was extensive in these events, so I want to do the prior testimony justice in terms of the summary for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If that is really a summary, we would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is a summary, albeit a long one, Mr. President. The witness served in the Royal Netherlands Army in various command and staff positions. He retired after 33 years in service with the rank of colonel. He arrived in Bosnia in January 1995 as a major and was the deputy commanding officer and logistics officer of DutchBat III, headquartered at Potocari. His immediate superior was the DutchBat commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. Beginning in April 1995, the VRS increased its firing upon DutchBat patrols and OPs. In addition, civilians were wounded by shelling and shooting and were taken to the Srebrenica hospital by DutchBat armoured ambulances. Colonel Franken described the DutchBat resupply process, which required VRS approval for both the contents and number of trucks in every convoy. In addition, the VRS categorically denied anything relating to weapons systems, spare parts, testing devices, ammunition, and communications equipment. The VRS restrictions on convoys increased after February, when the last fuel convoy was approved by the VRS. UNHCR was subject to the same approval process and restrictions by the VRS. Colonel Franken testified about the effect which the VRS restrictions on fuel convoys had on DutchBat's ability to carry out its mission: They had to patrol the enclave on foot and chop wood for heat; they could not keep their medical dressing station operational; nor could they purify water or cook food. They also had to close down their mobile Red Cross point in several villages, which gave medical care directly to the population. He further described how DutchBat's weapons and ammunition became severely reduced and inoperable because the VRS convoy restrictions prevented their necessary maintenance and replacement. He also testified about the VRS restrictions on DutchBat personnel rotations, such that when he arrived, the battalion's strength was over 300, but by July 1995 was down to 147 peacekeepers. Colonel Franken referred to these collective VRS convoy restrictions as "convoy terror." He also testified about the VRS attack on Observation Post Echo, OP Echo, by approximately 40 Serb infantry, supported by a T-55 battle tank, which forced the peacekeepers out of the OP after firing on it and striking its observation tower. Following this attack, Colonel Karremans described the critical situation of the battalion and the local population in a commander's assessment. Colonel Franken then described the VRS attack on the enclave that began on 6 July, including VRS direct firing on OPs, such as OP Foxtrot, in which a VRS tank blew away the OP's defence wall; random shelling of Srebrenica town; and firing at the UN Potocari compound and direct surroundings, resulting in civilian casualties. Because the VRS had not permitted the battalion operations officer to rotate back in, Colonel Franken assumed tactical command duties during the VRS attack and spent most of his time in the operations room. Nevertheless, he made rounds outside at least twice daily to see the situation for himself. He also discussed his 9 July order to form blocking positions with APCs to prevent further VRS penetration into the safe area and to force VRS the stay static enough to be struck by close air support. These APCs also came under direct VRS tank and artillery fire, resulting in one APC being shot off the road and shrapnel wounds and light injuries to DutchBat peacekeepers. A recovery vehicle sent to retrieve the APC came under fire from an anti-tank gun and a T-55 tank, and had to withdraw. By 10 July, there was massive shelling of Srebrenica, including the UN Bravo Company compound, resulting in further casualties. Colonel Franken further testified that the VRS issued an ultimatum to civilians, BiH soldiers, DutchBat, and UNHCR to leave by 0600 hours on 11 July. UNPROFOR responded with an ultimatum of its own that the VRS should withdraw to the so-called Morillon lines by 0600 the next morning or there would be massive air-strikes. By 11 July, however, the ABiH had disappeared, and the VRS had completely surrounded the OPs, and had infantry poised at heights around Srebrenica town as, one by one, the OPs continued to fall to the Serbs. Peacekeepers formerly manning OPs were taken to Bratunac where they were held prisoner by the VRS, not free leave. The civilian population was fleeing in great numbers from Srebrenica town to the Potocari compounds, with Bravo Company peacekeepers accompanying the column and bringing up the tail. And the column was shelled by mortar and artillery, the wounded being picked up along the way. Had the VRS wanted to kill everybody in that column, it could have done so. In total, 114 wounded were brought to Potocari. The peacekeepers guided the refugees towards the back of the Potocari compound and away from the road directly in front of it because Colonel Franken believed that if the refugees entered from the front, the VRS would fire upon them with an anti-tank gun, T-55 tank, and multiple rocket-launcher to the north of the compound near OP Papa. When the compound filled with refugees, they were directed to abandoned factories and a bus compound to the south. By the night of 11 July, they estimated there were between 800 and 1.000 Muslim men inside and outside the compound. After close air support was delivered in the afternoon of 11 July, Colonel Franken received a threat that if close air support continued, the VRS would shell the compound and the refugees there, and kill the peacekeepers held prisoner in Bratunac. He took the threat to shell the compound seriously, because the Serbs had used artillery before randomly on Srebrenica town, on the area of Potocari, and on the refugees fleeing Srebrenica for Potocari, and he thought that if they wanted to do it again, they probably would. Shortly after that threat, there was mortar shelling of the bus compound area and a full round from the multiple rocket system towards Potocari, resulting in wounded and panic among the refugees. In the morning of 12 July, he observed the Serb forces advancing towards Potocari from the north, and sometime after noon or around noon, a large number of buses and trucks began arriving. That day, he met two VRS Colonels, one named Acamovic, who identified himself as a logistics officer, and one named Jankovic, who identified himself as being from Pale and said his mission was to prepare and co-ordinate DutchBat's withdrawal. As the first buses had already started to leave, Colonel Franken assigned Major Boering and Captain Voerman to escort the first convoy. He received reports that the first and second convoy went well, but thereafter, the VRS stopped all of the UN escorts, thus taking away, as Colonel Franken put it, his eyes and ears.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The escorts were stripped of their vehicles, weapons, equipment and clothing in such a way that he concluded that it was organised and designed to prevent the UN from witnessing whatever happened to the convoys. He complained to Colonel Jankovic but did not see any results. Mladic had announced that men would be separated, so except for the first convoy, men were separated immediately after they left the perimeter secured by peacekeepers, and taken to the White House, from which they were transported in the direction of Bratunac. The Serbs consistently thwarted efforts to escort the buses containing men. In addition, the Serbs prevented peacekeepers from investigating the treatment of the men in the White House. He complained again, without results, to Colonel Jankovic. The men had to leave their belongings in front of the White House in a large pile, which the Serbs later burned. Colonel Franken also testified about efforts he made to register the men at the UN compound and informed Colonel Jankovic that he had done so. One of Colonel Franken's OP crews also reported seeing a large group of men kneeling on a soccer field, next to a road, in rows, with their hands on their necks. Colonel Jankovic had contacted Colonel Franken for a truck to bring that OP crew back. After the population was moved out, there were still wounded Muslims remaining in Potocari and in Bratunac. The Serbs wanted to keep them in Serb territory, but Franken contacted the ICRC and MSF to evacuate them. On 17 July, Colonel Jankovic led a Serb delegation, including Momir Nikolic, to arrange the evacuation of the wounded. After which Nikolic inspected the wounded at the hospital to determine whether they were soldiers or war criminals. Jankovic then summoned Nesib Mandzic and asked him and Colonel Franken to sign a declaration Jankovic produced that stated that the transportations had been performed according to international law and the Geneva Conventions. The declaration's content was nonsense because the population did not have a realistic opportunity to stay. Colonel Franken signed the declaration because Colonel Jankovic had indicated that doing so would facilitate the evacuation of the wounded. When an ICRC truck was stopped at the Serb border, during this meeting, Colonel Jankovic was able to resolve the problem with a single phone call. Mr. President, at this time I would also offer Exhibits P599 to 619, which are the exhibits admitted through Colonel Franken in the Popovic case or which were shown to him during the course of his testimony in Popovic but tendered through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They all will be received with exhibit numbers already given to them. Mr. Thayer, as everybody can see, we have a problem with the transcript of today, the transcript in e-court is different from that in LiveNote, not only the lines are different, but there are many obviously technical problems so that it will be quite difficult during the testimony of this witness to refer to several portions of the transcript, so that I conferred with the Registrar to figure out the possibility what to do. We should prefer to have a break now to resolve this problem so that we have a clear and reliable transcript. Sometimes the problems occurred on the left screen, sometimes on the right screen, there's no common understanding, so that, as I propose, we should have a break now in order to resolve this technical problem. Then we resume as soon as possible when the problem is solved. Thank you very much. We adjourn. --- Break taken at 9.26 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's start again. I hope the technical problems will be not as concerning as at the beginning. But I've heard, Mr. Thayer, that the interpreters didn't catch the last part of your witness summary, so that you should -- I've heard you have liaised with the B/C/S booth and know which part was missing, but especially for the accused, it's necessary to have the full text translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Colonel Franken also testified about efforts he made to register the men on the Potocari compound, compiling a list of men who were willing to have their names placed on it, and Colonel Franken told Colonel Jankovic that he had done so. One of Colonel Franken's OP crews also reported seeing a large group of men kneeling on a soccer field, next to a road, in rows, with their hands on their necks. Colonel Jankovic had contacted Colonel Franken for a truck to bring that OP crew back. After the population was moved out, there were still wounded Muslims remaining in Potocari and Bratunac. The Serbs wanted to keep them in Serb territory, but Franken contacted the ICRC via MSF to evacuate them. On 17 July, Colonel Jankovic led a Serb delegation, including Momir Nikolic, to arrange the evacuation of the wounded, after which Nikolic inspected the wounded to determine whether they were soldiers or war criminals. Jankovic then summoned Nesib Mandic and asked him and Colonel Franken to sign a declaration, which Jankovic produced, and which stated that the transportations had been performed according to international law and the Geneva Conventions. The declaration's content was nonsense because the population did not have a realistic opportunity to stay. Colonel Franken signed the declaration because Colonel Jankovic had indicated that doing so would facilitate the evacuation of the wounded. When an ICRC truck was stopped at the Serb border, Colonel Jankovic was able to resolve the problem with a single phone call. 1

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I have a few questions to put to you on three or four topics. The first concerns three borders around the enclave which you testified about in Popovic. You refer to them -- and for the record this is at transcript pages 2477 and 2645. You referred to three borders around the enclave. Would you please give the Trial Chamber a description of what you were referring to when you spoke about three borders.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I will. There was what I call the UN border said as well -- named as well as the Morillon Line. And there was with the Serbs quite another idea, that the border was up until 1 kilometre within the enclave that should have been the correct border. And the Muslims had the idea that the border was up to 1 kilometre outside the UN border. So in fact, there were more or less three enclaves, a UN enclave, that's what the Serbs considered as being border of the enclave and that what the Muslims considered being the enclave. Is that enough? Is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And was there a relationship between the UN border, as you described, and the location of the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The observation posts were on the -- mostly on the very edge of the UN border, so directly in front of the observation posts there was the UN border of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, was there ever one border that everybody agreed upon, the UN, the Serbs, and the Muslims, around the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. There should be formed a so-called Joint Commission, three parties, being UN, Serbs, and the Muslims, to agree upon the order of -- the border of the enclave. That never came to an actual situation because they didn't want to speak to each other, so it was pretty difficult to coordinate the exact consented border of the enclave. So we kept as to the UN border being the real one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Next topic, Colonel, Observation Post Echo. You testified in Popovic, and this is at transcript page 2452, about how on the 3rd of June, 1995, the VRS attacked that OP and forced the peacekeepers out of it. How was this information being relayed to you at the time, and how involved were you personally with the events concerning the VRS attack on OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: OP Echo was in the area of responsibility of my B Company, who was responsible for the southern part of the enclave. The OP reported to the company and the company to me, so I got the information through the HQ of the company, that in the morning there was some movement in front of the OP, which in the end showed -- proved to be an attack on Echo, about 40 infantry men supported by a T-55, that's a main battle tank, and then the anti-aircraft gun on the high ridge directly on the western part of that area. They asked me permission to withdraw. I did not give that permission. Because I wanted to be sure that that there was actually an attack and the Serbs opened fire, and the very last moment or the last possibility, I allowed the OP to withdraw which they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you say, "They asked me for permission to withdraw," who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Company asked me permission to withdraw that OP. Perhaps of any interest is that the Serbs, before they started the attack, summoned the OP crew to leave the OP, and they did that by means of a loud-speaker, in English. Which we refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for the Trial Chamber the design, the size, the appearance of these OPs, to give the Trial Chamber an idea of what we are talking about when we talk about one of these observations posts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The observation posts were, in fact, militarily seen, a complete joke. Because they were out in the open, on the top of hills or directly in a valley, where they, in fact, didn't hardly see anything because they had to deter by presence. They had to be seen by all parties that we were there. They were painted white and by night we had to put on lights on it so that even at night everybody could see that UN was there. So the military position was absolutely ridiculous. For instance, Echo was down on the road, 5 metres on the left side, there was a slope up to 10 metres, and woods on it, on the right side there were bushes and a part of a river and buildings. And that is not a position which you would choose if you reckoned with defending that position, because that is absolutely idiotic. You can't control the approaches and you can't can be outmanoeuvred on your left and right flank whenever the opponent wants because you can't fire in that area. You can't bring your weapons to action, in fact, to that area. So the aim of the observation post was only to show the flag, to show that we were there. But then again, a military defence position, I would have fired the officer that would have chosen that location to defend that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this will probably come up during your testimony and throughout the trial, so can you briefly explain the difference between what we refer to sometimes as indirect fire and direct fire? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, direct fire is when the gun or the weapons system directly sees the target and fires on it. Indirect firing is, for instance, artillery or mortars who fire in a - what do you call it? - a bow. And mostly is led by an observer which controls and corrects that fire. So the indirect firing, the weapons system can't see the target and fires at it on indication of an observer or on a coordinate, but that gets a bit technical now. Direct firing is, for instance, a tank seeing a target, firing at that target. Is that enough an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. The reports that you were receiving concerning the attack on OP Echo, were you getting report that this was direct fire or indirect fire on that OP?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Reports as I recollect were direct firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the damage, if any, that was done to the OP?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know the tower, the observation tower, was hit, was a big hole in that. And the defence wall was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you refer to a defence wall, Colonel. What is a defence wall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, some kind of a container existing of metal threads and filled with small rocks and sand, about the height of about 2 metres and the width is about 150. And in general, it protects against direct firing. Initially, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just follow up on that, what do you mean by "initially"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Because if you keep on firing on a defence wall by a heavy weapons system, like a main battle tank, you'll blow the defence wall away. That's what I meant with "initially." The first hit it can manage, second probably as well, but a third hit, it's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When this attack on OP Echo occurred, Colonel, did you seek any support from the higher command in the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We thought that the conditions for air support were fulfilled and we asked for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why did you feel justified in seeking air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was a direct attack on UN facilities, on UN troops. The Serbs were entering the enclave and that were both -- and there were what they called smoking guns, which meant that there was an actual fire contact. And that were three of the conditions UN had for allowing air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how important was air support to you and your mission, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: My initial mission was, of course, to deter by presence, so we were not equipped to -- for a real fight, nor weapons systems, nor the number of troops I had. So to equalise the lack of fire-power I had on the ground, I absolutely needed air support to give enough fire-power to do the job, being there and defending an OP or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you said equalise, what did you need to equalise to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The lack, the lack of fire-power I had compared to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from your experience, from what you could see from the VRS side, how much of a concern to the VRS was the potential of NATO air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, just reread that question. Well, in other regions, they showed that they -- it was proved that they were pretty -- under the impression of air support were more or less petrified when that came in. So I thought again that it was a very good means to stop that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in Popovic, and this is at transcript 2450, about a meeting you had with the Muslim military leadership about what DutchBat would do and what the Muslim forces in the area would do in the event of a VRS full-on attack on the enclave. What prompted that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I could not completely coordinate any action in case of an attack because I was still a UN unit and supposed to be, not only supposed to be, but I was impartial, so I couldn't take a side before things happened. Through a pretty complicated discussion, we concluded that UN would, as ordered by the UN, would defend its OPs, and the BiH would cope with the area between the OPs without a really fire co-ordinated fight, because I was not allowed to do that. But in fact, we said, We'll defend the OPs, and the BiH said, Okay, then we'll defend the area between the OPs. OPs being observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this meeting was before or after the attack on OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So was there anything in particular that prompted this meeting that you had concerning what you might do in an event of an attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the period, but somewhere in beginning of May, this meeting took place on the initiative of the Chief of Staff of the 28th Muslim Division. And they thought that a Serb attack was evident in that time. Well, we didn't have any indication that that was correct, but after that being established, we had this discussion. They thought the Serbs would come in and were, of course, curious what DutchBat would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there any relationship between the increase in close firing incidents in which DutchBat patrols and OPs had been fired at by VRS soldiers or positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As stated before, there was a pretty massive increase in firing at our patrols and at certain OPs. But to us, that was not a direct indication that an attack would be evident. Probably for the BiH it was or they had information I didn't because, you know, the normal military intelligence did absolutely not work there. I got no information whatsoever from the UN about troop movements or whatever the Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during the attack on OP Echo, what happened to any elements of Bosnian Muslim forces that may have been in the area, if they were in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were in the area, but what proved to be later on a kind of bad habit, they -- we, in that discussion which I had with the Chief of Staff of 28th, we agreed that the Muslim forces would inform us when they would withdraw from their positions, logically, because otherwise my OPs were defending, like, just one little spot surround by Serbs, and that is a bad thing to do. But the first time at Echo, the BiH disappeared without notifying us and that is why the Serbs got the opportunity to come that close and come on my flanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when the VRS was firing directly at the OP, were there Muslim forces in or near the OP such that the Serbs might have been firing at them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. There were no BiH soldiers in positions in that area that could interfere with the fight or the attack on Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in Popovic at transcript 2455, about a commander's assessment which Colonel Karremans sent following the increase in firing incidents and the attack on OP Echo, and as you put it, the increasing vulnerability of the Swedish Shelter Project. Did you have an opportunity recently to read a copy of that assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did read it, yes. It coped with my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: 4th of June. As far as I know, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall to whom Colonel Karremans sent that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He sent that to UN headquarters in Sarajevo and a copy went to the Sector North-east, which officially was our direct higher echelon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Sector North-east, where is that based, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What in particular do you recall about that report, if anything stands out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, he described the situation. He described the attack. He assessed what the meaning of that attack was. That far is normal. And he described the position of the state the battalion was in, and by that I mean the absolute lack weapons system, heavy weapons systems, ammunition, the lack of fuel, et cetera, so the logistic situation with all these limitations to the operational possibilities. And he described the situation of the people of the enclave, the civil people, being a very bad situation because there was hardly any food, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there will probably be some reference in the future to the Swedish Shelter Project. Can you just briefly describe what that is for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, before DutchBat III came in, and I don't know exactly when it was built, it was built by an NGO in a kind of village with barracks. And in those barracks there were housing about 3.000 refugees, being people that came to the enclave from the area outside the enclave in 1992, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just roughly, geographically in the enclave, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: About 800 metres west of OP Echo, direct north of Delta and Kilo. So let's say, in general the southeastern part of the enclave. South, southeastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll look at a map in a couple of minutes with those OPs on them. I want to turn your attention now to the period of the actual VRS attack on the enclave. And I want to show you P621, which actually, I don't think we looked at during your proofing, but I think you can handle it, Colonel. Tell me when you see it on your screen and when you've had an opportunity to familiarise yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I see some text on the right side. And as far as I can see it is, yeah, another assessment of Colonel Karremans. Just hold. I more or less read the first four points and it looks like an assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just go to page 2, if we could, and then we'll go back to page 1 after you've had a chance to look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Very small. Okay. I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, how personally familiar are you with the topics that are discussed in this report from Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I didn't read this one before but the assessment is correct. I didn't read or know about his advices in the point 10, that's new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go back to page 1 and we'll focus on some particular points in this report. We can see that it's dated 9 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Colonel Karremans starts out by talking about, as of Thursday, 6 July, the VRS, he refers to it as BSA, but we'll continue to refer to it as VRS, started offensive operations, shelling OPs, battalion headquarters, Srebrenica itself, and refers to civilian casualties. Were you, yourself, personally receiving reports of this activity, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, because the ops room directly -- the ops room, sorry, that is the nerve centre of the battalion where all the information came in, operations room. And I always got directly the information from that operation room. Mostly in these days summaries, but I can confirm that this happened. And I mean the events as described in 1, and 2, and 3, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 2, he refers to attacking ABiH, that's Muslim Army, and UN positions, shelling the enclave and suppressing DutchBat through intimidation by using artillery, mortars, and MLRS, overhead compound Potocari with over 200 soldiers. First of all, what's MLRS stand for, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Multiple launch rocket system. It's a system with - what do you call that? - pipes on it where rockets are in and they are able to give, this type, as I remember well, eight rockets at a time, which covers an area of 400 by 400 metres in a devastating way, for soft targets, of course. Is that too military technical or is that an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think somebody will let you know if it's too much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a modern version of the old RussianKatyushas, some people know that. Stalinorgel or Stalin organ they called it in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Perhaps that makes it clear what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Karremans goes on and he says: "Most of my OPs have been shot by mortars."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "BSA does exactly know what they are doing, until how far they can go. They do execute their operations according to a predominated and well-organised plan." Based on your observations, the information you are receiving, your experience there at the time, what is Colonel Karremans saying here? What is he communicating to the higher command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He is communicating that, to his conviction and mine, it was a co-ordinated plan and there were patterns recognisable in firing. It was clear that they were firing and shooting at the area of the HQ for intimidation, which happened in the same time as shelling our OPs, and that can't be incidental or something, that must have been co-ordinated and ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when he refers to "until how far they can go," what is he talking about there and what do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably -- but as I don't know because I don't know what his -- the reasons or his arguments were to say this, but it is an assumption what I'm doing now. I think that he meant that, in this day then, we already knew that the BSA had quite a lot of artillery mortars, and that they were trying to give just that amount of fire to immobilise DutchBat and to try to make us prepared to surrender or to stop fighting or to stop opposing them. I think that is what he meant. But again, we didn't discuss this and I have to try to find arguments why he said that. But that is what I see as a reason for this remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, he writes that: "Yesterday at 1400 hours, OP F, Foxtrot, did receive another three hits by T-55, while ABiH positions were already left due to heavy fighting and have been disabled." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I said that about Echo, the first time that the ABiH left the positions on our flanks without telling us so. This is the second time they did that. And so the OP Foxtrot was, as we call it, in the air, alone, on the top of a hill, in sight for every weapons system the VRS could bring up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what effect that direct tank firing --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, the northern part of the defence wall, north-eastern part of the defence wall was blown away, so they were in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of this document, sir. If we look at paragraph 6, we see a reference to the Swedish Shelter Project in the south being shelled. Is that what you were talking about a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same project I was talking about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7 under the heading "Commander's Assessment," Colonel Karremans refers to the VRS taking positions around Zeleni Jadar and what he expects them to do next, and he says, "I did express these concerns already last month." Does that reference to expressing his concerns last month refer to any particular report, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, but again we talked about that before, the increase of close firing and pressure and, well, violence at the VRS site was not direct reason for us to think they would attack the -- on short term attack the enclave, but we thought that the situation was deteriorating. And I think he -- without any doubt, he reported that to the higher echelon, and that's what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the transcript, I note that what is written here says, "close firing and pressure and violence at the VRS site." Is that what you meant to say or did you mean to say something else than at the VRS site?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's strange to say, but he meant probably by the VRS, but he wrote at the VRS site. But this is what I meant to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, paragraph 10, Colonel Karremans says that: "Using close air support, CAS, in all possible ways is, in my opinion, not feasible yet. It will provoke the BSA in such a way that both Srebrenica itself and OPs and compounds will be targeted by all means." Then he refers to: "Especially the MLRS north of OP P, Papa, the MLRS within Bratunac, and all their artillery and mortars will launch their missiles and rounds at fixed targets. Unless these weapons systems could be eliminated in once, which is hardly impossible." Can you explain whether you and Colonel Karremans had discussions about what is contained in this paragraph, and if you could expand on what this paragraph means a little bit for the Trial Chamber, please, especially in regards to what you were facing at this period during the VRS attack?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Having read it completely now, I think it's based on advice I gave. I happened to be close air support specialist for armored infantry brigade. And what he referring to is that it's great to have an aeroplane destroy one tank, but the consequence will be that the VRS will use all its artillery to respond, so the only way to do this is take their hardware, their artillery and their tanks, as far as we knew where they were, take them out, then close air support is evident again. And that's -- probably we'll come to that, that's the story of the air-strike, why we gave later the advice and asked for an air-strike, it's an air request where we gave all the targets we knew with the request to wipe them out in a short period. To make clear what I mean, if there are 30 guns, artillery pieces or mortars or whatever, and you take just one out, the other will respond and fire increasingly with the same damage. So it's little use to take out just that one piece. The VRS had, compared to us, an overwhelming amount of artillery and we, ourselves, didn't have weapons systems to cope with that. We couldn't attack them because they were out of sight and it didn't have anything to reach them. So the only way then to neutralise the plus and fire-power the VRS had compared to us, is take all their hardware, all their artillery you know of, take them out in one big blow and then you are pretty successful in getting even -- more or less even amounts of fire-power at our side and the VRS side. I hope I made myself clear because it's getting a bit technical, but I can't help that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, but the sum and effect what he says here is, close air support is not feasible yet, we shoot, do an air-strike, take all their hardware out, and then when they come with a single tank or some tanks or what, then we can use close air support. And that, I suppose, is based on a discussion he had with me about air support. I hope I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to the term "forward air controller." Just briefly, what is that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There are a lot of possibilities to oppose the -- your enemy with air support. One of them is close air support, what that does mean is that the enemies came quite close to your own positions, so to prevent the pilots of making mistakes, and by mistakes I mean attack own troops and not the enemy, there's an observer who has contact with the plane and leads him to that target. And that's called a forward air controller. The other system is battle-field air interdiction, and that is what we meant later on with the air-strike. Then their own troops can't see the target but know where it is, and the pilot finds it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a map, and is P00104, please. This is page 8, please, of the map book. If we could scroll down and if it's possible to blow up the purple ring area that's marked with the letters a little bit, maybe centre that if we could in the -- blow up and centre it a little bit in the screen. Perfect. Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I think we'll all agree what we are looking at is a map that shows the locations of the UN OPs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to do something a little probably imprecise for your taste, but if you could take the pen that's connected to the computer there, the Trial Chamber has seen now various references in your testimony and the documents to these weapons systems, those VRS weapons systems that were located to the north of the Charlie Company compound at Potocari, the UN base in Potocari, near OP Papa, I think you said. Can you just draw some lines to indicate where these weapons systems were and what their line of fire was, whether it was a direct line or indirect line of fire. You referred in your testimony, for example, to not wanting the refugees to enter the front of the compound because you were afraid that they would be fired upon. If you could just identify the locations of those weapons systems, maybe with a 1, 2, and 3, and define which each was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'll try. There was a high edge here, that is, I'll try, number 1, being the anti-tank gun sitting in a saddle on that high ridge, having view and possibility and did fire like this. But again, it's pretty inaccurate what I'm doing now. Directly northwest of it was the position that, I'll number that 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I leaned forward too much. Position 2 is one of the positions the main battle tank had, the T-55, but that switched positions oftentimes, which is usual. But that is the initial position, and the multiple launch rocket system was around here, as far as we know. The tank, the number 1 and number 2 had a view and a reach or a fire zone more or less given on the map by the red lines. And the multiple launch rocket system is a system which fires indirectly. As far as I know, the reach of that system was, in fact, the complete enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've indicated that MLRS system with a circle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'll put 3 in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: But we didn't know the exact position. We extracted that from the times that he fired. So on hearing of the firing, we guessed his position. It's somewhere in that area. We didn't see the thing actually because it was behind that high ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we are done with this. If we could save it and I would tender this exhibit at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take the opportunity to do something that I forgot when you tendered several documents with this witness. The documents P606, P608, P610, P618, and P619 have no translation yet. So these will be marked pending translation. We must have our first break now, I think, and during the break, the system shall be restarted so that have we no longer any problems with it. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Two quick issues. First is, we will be able to have our witnesses here, given the change in the schedule. We might have to change the order around, because of flights and so forth, but it will be the same witnesses and we'll be able to fill the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Number two is, I'm mindful of the time I estimated for this witness and I've already exceeded it. I've reduced some of the areas I had for Colonel Franken further, but I do seek the Court's permission for some additional time with Colonel Franken. I think some of these issues are, I hope, helpful to the Trial Chamber, and I'd like to continue with the areas I have to cover with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you give an indication about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think it's going to be another half an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This seems not to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, good morning again, Colonel. You testified about the direct firing by this T-55 tank at OP Foxtrot, blowing away its defence wall. Again, you spoke about the situation at OP Echo a month earlier. Let me ask you again, with respect to this direct firing by the tank, given your experience as a trained infantry officer, is there any way that OP Foxtrot was fired at accidently by the VRS on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The distance that Tango 55 from the OP was about 150, 200 metres. Alas, we didn't have means to deal with that tank because I didn't have any anti-tank weapons anymore. But from a distance of about 150 up to 200 metres, on an OP which is completely in the open, without any targets in the area, it can't be by accident. That would be nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you request close air support or air support of any kind that day, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: On Foxtrot we did again, yes, because we did that many times, but -- and I don't know what excuse there was on this occasion, but we didn't get it. There were several reasons given by the UN why air support was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, what were some of those reasons, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were no planes available. They didn't consider it as an attack or a heavy attack enough to justify air support. The other reason I got was that, to their opinion, my own infantry and the Serb infantry were mixed, so air support was impossible, which was nonsense, et cetera. Reasons like that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, what was your justification for requesting air support at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: More or less the same reasons. Direct attack on a UN unit, Serbs entering the enclave, well, that were the main reasons and that coped with the conditions the UN had for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think we are all agreed that shortly after that direct fire at the OP Foxtrot, Private Van Renssen was killed by ABiH fire. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why DutchBat didn't request any kind of air support with respect to the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The killing of Private Van Renssen was when OP Foxtrot withdrew to his base again, being B Company in Srebrenica. The fact that ABiH fired at DutchBat couldn't be seen as a real attack. Perhaps I should explain that. ABiH had massive disciplinary problems. Local commanders did exactly what they would and not what the division said. It led even to us picking up the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, brought him into the line of fighting to get his local commanders to reason. So this was a tragedy, in fact, but we saw it as an incident because there was not -- you couldn't speak of an organised attack or whatever. It was, alas, a BiH, more or less, soldier who went bananas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, other than the OP structures themselves, you've described damage to the watch-tower, the observation tower, the defence wall getting blown away on another one. Did DutchBat lose any particular pieces of equipment to direct VRS firing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recollect, one or two unarmed vehicles, jeeps, and three APCs. That's correct, three APCs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to show you another document, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is P602. I've been told by our language people that both the English and the B/C/S translations which we have and are trying to improve are a little rough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what I'd like to ask to you do, Colonel, is simply to read --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have the Dutch original on the screen. It's a pretty short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I could ask to you simply read the essential text of this document and explain to the Trial Chamber what it's about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is information for Captain Groen, being the commander of B Company, the company stationed in the south part and his base camp in the city of Srebrenica. And that concerned a message we got from the BSA, sorry, VRS and an ultimatum we got from the VRS and a UN reaction with an ultimatum to the VRS. Why in writing? Because I was pretty busy in the location of our headquarters so I couldn't go in the direction of the captain, and I wouldn't like to use the command net radio communications we had for messages like this because he was busy leading his company, and then you don't interfere with messages like this on his command net. It comes to the fact that the other commanders were by hand, they were all stationed with their HQs in Potocari, quite next to my own HQ, so I could tell them, and Captain Groen, commander B Company, had to be informed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to just translate what you've written here in this in this message to the captain with respect to the VRS ultimatum? What was the ultimatum here that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the VRS gave us a message by radio saying, The UN did not or doesn't disarm the ABiH so we will do that as of 11, 600 hours. 11 is the date, 600 hours is 6 o'clock in the morning. Plus 48 hours. Civilians, soldiers of ABiH, so Muslim soldiers, and DutchBat, turn in their weapons and leave the enclave through Yellow Bridge. Yellow Bridge is a location in the north of the enclave, the entrance of the enclave next to that Observation Post Papa you saw before on the map. The reaction of the UN, you want that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The UN then sent ultimatum to the VRS. VRS is to withdraw after the lines -- behind the lines of Morillon, being our UN border I described before, with [indiscernible] it says the old enclave as we -- that looked as we came in. "Every VRS attack has to be stopped. As of 600 hours tomorrow morning the withdrawal has to start. If not," the text stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think what happened in the last trial was either we didn't have the second page or we forgot about the second page but we didn't talk about the second page, although you talked about the substance of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if we could go to page 2 of the original Dutch, which hopefully will be in the system. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think at the top it says: "If not," and if you could translate for us.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: "Massive air attacks on all VRS targets in and around the enclave. Mission as of 600 hours, take cover." It's a normal procedure when you get massive air support, then you have to -- everything that is not necessary outside, you want them in cover. "Vehicles without the compounds marked." Marked is with orange flags on the top of a vehicle, so all the pilots can recognise own troops. That is a NATO procedure, and that is done again when close air support is delivered so the pilot can't make a mistake who is the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: And then it's underlined, it's a mistake or repeating of the same message probably printed and there is a cross through it, but it's the same text as at page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this refers to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I forgot one. There's a note then writ: "Your mission to defend the city is still evident."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the original VRS ultimatum spoke about, as you said, by 0600 on the 11th of July, plus 48 hours, everybody leaves. So what day did you send this message to the captain?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Oh, that's good question, just try to recollect that. I suppose it is the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender P602 at this time. Is that already in? That's one of the original documents. Being redundant, I'll withdraw that request, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. But perhaps you can tell us if there's an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is. There is an English translation, again though it's -- I'm being told by our language people that it's a little rough, so we'll get a better one and upload that as soon as possible, and it's being worked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case we should mark it for identification, pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I guess technically, Mr. President, page 2 of this document was not part of, from what I can see, the original document in Popovic. So maybe I need to formally tender it now just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The second page will be part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, during these events, this VRS attack on the enclave, things were clearly moving pretty quickly. You are receiving a lot of information, making a lot of decisions, making a lot of calls, receiving a lot of information and reports. How confused were you, was DutchBat, about who was shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was not confused about who was shooting at me. There were some incidents with BiH, but without shooting at us, where they didn't allow us to withdraw or to move with our vehicles. But the shooting was quite clear to me it was done by the VRS, and to DutchBat as well, not only me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when Private van Renssen was killed, you knew that that was by the BiH and not by anybody else, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How were your communications functioning during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: With my units, good. At least the units that were not taken POW by the VRS, but with my units, with my companies, it was perfect. No problem. We had some problems with communications to the higher echelons, but they were not severe that we couldn't speak or for a longer time didn't have any communications to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in Popovic that Mladic had announced that there would be separation of the men. This was at transcript page 2496. When did you first hear, to the best of your recollection, that General Mladic had made this announcement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Could have been the night of the 11th, when Colonel Karremans came back from his second meeting, but I'm sure I heard it on the debrief on the 12th, when he came back from his final meeting. But I -- as far as I recollect, I already knew about that the 11th, late.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall any particular ages that were mentioned, age range of men that would be separated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Men from 16 up till 60. 1-6 till 6-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've testified and we've spoken about today this Colonel Jankovic, and I want to show you a photograph. We are going to do this on Sanction as opposed to e-court and just ask you if you recognise any of the people in the picture. If you can tell the Trial Chamber who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this, for the record, is P624.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right side is the -- by -- mentioned by you the Colonel Jankovic, and the left side it's quite clear who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender P624 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness, you didn't mention the name of that man --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, on the left side was Mladic. Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Jankovic ever tell you what his actual position was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, he did not. He introduced himself as being the officer, again, from Pale. They all said they came from Pale. And his job was to coordinate and make arrangements for the withdrawal of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him to try to find out what his actual position was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Of course I did, but I didn't get an answer. Answers like, Well, it's not evident, it's not important, my job now is clear, I hope, et cetera. Answers like that. He never gave his correct position on what staff or what function.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, from what command level did you understand Colonel Jankovic to be from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Main Staff, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after the -- well, I'll withdraw that and save some time. Did Colonel Jankovic ever provide you with information about what was going on outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, he was the one that informed me that the -- the Muslims, being parts of the 28th Division plus plus, and -- broke out of the enclave in northern direction and had contact with the VRS. And by that occasion, he reported to me that they already had about 6.000 prisoners taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Colonel Jankovic referred to any particular location when he referred to that break-out and taking those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, not -- I do not remember a city or a town or something like that, but I know he said that they broke out from the enclave in northern direction and that's the information he gave. I don't recollect villages or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just quote you a section from your OTP statement and see if this refreshes your recollection, whether you agree with it or not. This is from page 7 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S. We don't need to put it up on e-court but it's P607 if anybody wants to check. You say in that statement that: "Jankovic told me that the BH Army had tried to get through Kasaba and then further on to the north in the direction of Zvornik." Does that refresh your recollection about the location?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds a bell but I couldn't remember at the very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now, Colonel, to the issue of the evacuation of the wounded people who remained at the Potocari compound and some of whom were also at the hospital in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in that connection, if we could see P626, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What we have here is a report from Colonel Jankovic to the Main Staff intelligence and security sector. I want to focus your attention on paragraph 1. Colonel Jankovic refers to the completion of the removal of the entire Muslim population, and then he refers to the numbers of wounded who remained. Do you see where it says: "A list of names has been taken from the UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you comment on that at all, Colonel? Do you know anything about a list of the names of wounded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, because we tried to get them out by UN means which was a NORMEDCOY, a Norwegian unit being in the area of Tuzla who was supposed to get the wounded out. We had to start a procedure of asking permission for a permission of a convoy again and an absolute demand was then that there were lists with the exact names of every person, being UN member or not, in that convoy. That's the reason why they had that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go down a little further in that paragraph, it reads: "The deputy commander of the battalion has told me that he will try to arrange this with international humanitarian organizations so that their medical treatment can continue in the FRY." Now, and we see immediately after that that Colonel Jankovic is recommending that they -- those wounded be transferred to Zvornik to get treatment there. Why did you want to arrange for an international organisation to take over those wounded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Because I wanted them without the grip or influence of the VRS, and the international organisation was because the UN units, Norwegian Medical Company, tried to reach us but they did not succeed crossing the CL in their area -- sorry, confrontation line in their area, whether that was by fire or whatever. But I was reported that it was impossible for the UN unit to come and evacuate those wounded. As I said before, I didn't want them to come into the hands of the VRS. The only solution was try the ICRC to get them out, International Red Cross. And through MSF I finally succeeded in arranging that. MSF is Medecins Sans Frontieres, an NGO.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why didn't you want those wounded to be in the custody of the VRS, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Experience we had. We tried to bring the wounded out during the evacuation. We had a hell of a lot of trouble at the crossing point in the area of Kladanj. People were beaten, bandages were taken from the people to see whether they were really wounded or not, and they were sent back. That is where a couple of them landed in Bratunac because the Serbs took them out, and just a few of them, of which one died already, came back to the camp. So having that experience, I absolutely didn't want those wounded in the hands of the VRS. I hope that's an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there -- did you have any concerns for their overall physical safety at that point, and if so, what was the basis of the concern?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, that is what I tried to explain. Seeing -- having experience how the VRS handled those wounded, I didn't have a reason to believe that it would be different if I handed them over now, and I wanted those people in security. So the only way to do that is bring them out of -- through the VRS area, out of that area, and it could only be done by the ICRC, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by that time, on or about the 17th of July, had you received any reports of executions or other atrocities that had been committed by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, proven were nine dead in the vicinity of our main gate, west of the so-called White House, a building right in front of our main gate. We had a report of the execution of one man by two VRS soldiers in the area of the bus station, just out of the parameter of the UN at that time. And there were, of course, all kinds of rumours but not proven. Every time when we got a report out of the civil population, we tried or we went out to see whether executions had been performed or there were dead, but we never found them. And then again, it was not that far because we were not allowed or it was impossible to go out, by occasion, 400 or 500 metres out of the compound because then our patrols were blocked by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go back up to this first paragraph. Colonel Jankovic writes that: "A doctor from the UNPROFOR has stayed in the hospital in Bratunac at the request of the hospital staff, to make sure that the patients are properly treated. I intend to send him away tomorrow, under the pretext that his help is not necessary." Do you have any knowledge, sir, whether that actually happened on or about the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It did not. That happened -- no, he was not sent away, but the wounded he was supposed to watch over. That's why we left him there. I don't know anything about a request of the hospital staff. We left him there to watch over the wounded to be sure that they were treated properly. Later than 13th of July, and I don't recollect exactly the date, he was called away for a lunch, invited for a lunch with the hospital staff. And when he came back the wounded were gone. That made his job there oblivious.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified about this meeting that was led by Colonel Jankovic on the 17th of July, regarding the evacuation of these wounded. Is it fair to say that this was sort of a two-part process that day; the first part having to do with identifying the wounded who were actually going to be permitted to leave and then a second part dealing with something else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, the reason for that -- that meeting was to transfer the wounded to the ICRC and arrange or coordinate the actual leave of the wounded of the VRS area and, of course, my compound. Nikolic, Major Nikolic, Bratunac Brigade, insisted on checking the wounded, whether there were soldiers amongst them, and he demanded that they were then -- should have been -- wrongly, sorry, I correct. That they should be handled like POWs. ICRC consented that inspection. I sent some of my soldiers along. And in the time that inspection took place, Jankovic presented to my surprise, a declaration which he spoke of before, a declaration in which the representative of the civil population, in this case being Mr. Mandzic, declared that everything went according to rules and nothing happened during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look at that in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I'd like to tender P626, which is the report of Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. And at this point in time, I would like to take you back to a tendered photograph, P624. I was told that this whole document contains 105 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We are at this time seeking only to tender that one photograph. I think at a later time, you will hear testimony from one of our investigators about how that book was put together. For the time being, we would tender just that page

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To make the situation very clear, it should be uploaded as a single document, this photo, and it will be received with a separate document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, Your Honour, I think what we'll do, it might be easier, if we could, just to MIF it and then wait until we get the whole thing in evidence through the investigator so we don't have little bits and pieces with different numbers. If it's all the same to the Trial Chamber, if we just MIF it for the time being, and then when we get the whole thing in it will be part of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm told that it is already marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll just status quo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart has let me know that I also neglected to tender P621, which was the 9 July report sent by Colonel Karremans to his superior command, and Colonel Franken looked at that and testified about that a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as P621.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could look at P28, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just told us that Colonel Jankovic shows up at this meeting for the evacuation, to arrange the evacuation of these wounded and he produces a declaration. And if we could take a look at it, I don't want to go over it in much detail since it's in the Popovic transcript, but it's dated the 17th of July. That's four days after the last of the population had been removed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see here --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could scroll down just a little bit. Actually, if we can go to the next page in English. I see that this has been -- and the page after that. There should be a version that you signed, I can see it's been uploaded in a slightly different order. If we can go to the next page, please, in English. Okay. Let's try 65 ter 20 because that might have the full version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm told, Mr. Thayer, that is this is exactly the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the same number of pages, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So, unfortunately, we've not uploaded every pages of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In any event, then we can see here on the unsigned version that it says on Jankovic's declaration: "No incidents were provoked by any side during the evacuation, and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the International Law of War." And you added something in your own handwriting: "As far as convoys actually escorted by UN forces are concerned." What did you try to achieve by writing that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The text preliminary to my handwritten sentence was, in fact, nonsense because it was not correct. Colonel Jankovic gave to me that the signing of this declaration was, well, more or less a condition to get the wounded out properly. So by adding this sentence in, to my opinion, I made this document worthless because I say all the, I would almost say, bullshit mentioned before does only concern the convoys escorted by UN forces, and as you know by former testimony, we were only able to escort the first and second convoy. And that is correct, the first and second convoy nothing happened. So that is what I meant by adding this sentence because there were incidents we couldn't escort because we couldn't see happened to the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, now we have the second page in B/C/S on the screen with three signatures. Perhaps you can clarify the handwritten portion above the signatures. It seems to be in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, there is a version that was translated on the spot, I think as Colonel Franken has testified, that he wrote in English on -- this language that we see translated on the right, and then that was in turn translated into the B/C/S at the time on this copy that you see here. What I was hoping to be able to show Your Honours was the copy of the English translation, which was done at the time that Colonel Franken wrote his sentence in English but we don't have that right now, but we can certainly get that soon enough for you. So that's what we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel Franken, can you comment on that all and is that accurate? Or do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can't see whether the text in B/C/S is accurate but I can recognise my signing it, my name, and on the left on the side of that B/C/S page, and I know there's an English version that is a look-a-like, only in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask, who did this handwriting in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My interpreters. To be brief about it and perhaps for your information, Jankovic presented that declaration in B/C/S to me, so I said, Well, I can't read that. So I had my own UN interpreters translate it in an English version, and then I added in handwriting that sentence we spoke about and he wrote it in the B/C/S translation, the same sentence, but in Bosnian Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned a few moments ago that you tried to make this declaration worthless by --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- by adding the language that you added. Whether you added anything to this declaration or not, and let's just focus, for example, on this reference to the Serbs -- the Serbian side observing the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and international law. Based on what you observed and what you had reported to you at the time, how does this invocation of the Geneva Conventions and the international law square with what you saw and what you had reported to you was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I could compress my comment to nonsense. It's incorrect. Some of the -- I can give some examples. We had those nine deaths, we had the execution at the -- proven execution at the bus station. The time my patrols could get into the house because we want to check how they were treated, we cut some men loose who were hung to the ceiling at their thumbs, we cut them loose and then stayed around.
