I had my UNMOs, sorry, United Nations Military Observers, who were not under my command but there was a team of UNMOs within the enclave, I had them check at least how many men went in and how many went out. There was -- in fact they were treated badly. I gave you one example. And when we tried to control that and to correct that, in the end or pretty soon we were blocked by armed Serb soldiers, number about 40, who absolutely blocked over the street our approach to that house. So only these examples is for me a reason to say that the declaration is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you identify for the Trial Chamber the various issues about which you complained to Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I complained to Jankovic about the treatment of the men in the White House, about the fact that we were not able to control that, to be present, although we were -- initially we were allowed to escort and to control the whole evacuation. I complained about him -- to him about the robbing of my escort teams and the losing of weapons and vehicles. I asked him why still there were not medical supplies allowed to be brought in, because we were out of it. I asked him and complained about the fact that any logistic transport could take place now to improve the situation for the civil population as well because they needed water, for instance, and I didn't have any, or hardly. Well, all these, probably there are a lot more of examples, but just for the record. I complained and spoke to him or made him responsible for all things that went wrong in my opinion. And if the next question is did anything happen, no. He said, I'll see to it, I'll see in that. Nothing happened. One of his answers was, Well, we are another army than your army, orders are not always followed by everybody, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on your interactions with him, Colonel, did you believe that he didn't have the power to influence the situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, his point of view was, I'm only here to coordinate the withdrawal of DutchBat so all the other things is not my piece of cake and I can inform the commanders doing that, but, yeah, I don't know whether they do anything with it. And I do not believe that if he really wanted he couldn't. There's a nice example where with one phone call he had that ICRC truck pass the border within minutes, which meant to me that he had influence. He could obviously give orders which were followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified in Popovic about seeing Nesib Mandzic, one of the Muslims who had been selected to represent the community during the meetings with General Mladic, after he returned from the second Fontana meeting in the evening of 11 July and that he was in a state of panic. Do you recall the -- one of the other representatives, a woman whose first name was Camila?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to her, basically after this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: She was one of the three members of that committee that should and would represent the civil population, the Muslims in our area. And on my request, that committee was registering the men within the UN parameter. We spoke of that before. When she came out of our camp to register the men in the area of the bus station, she was provoked or handled by the VRS in that way that she -- well, she broke down. After that she was a patient in the hospital as well. She was completely, yeah, what do you say, off the world. She was intimidated in such a way that she really broke down, completely. And she went, in the end, out as a patient when the battalion went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions for you, Colonel. In connection with your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, do you recall reviewing a large stack of UNMO and UNPROFOR reports dated 6 July through the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall at that time reading them and being asked to indicate which -- whether each report appeared to you to be authentic and whether each report accurately described the events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me show you P623, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would kindly ask that we be given a reference as to where these excerpts are in the Milosevic transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll have to get back to the Court to give you that exact cite about where it is in the Milosevic transcript. I don't think there's any question that in connection with that case, Colonel Franken was shown these UNMO reports and confirmed, in this document that we see, its contents, but I'll get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No dispute about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- but it is necessary to have the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll see if I can get the reference for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, we have here an itemisation of these UNMO reports that you reviewed, and we can see your comments. Are those your initials in the lower right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that your signature there, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you stand by the comments that you made and are contained in this document about these UNMO reports, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender P623 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received with this P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now lastly, Colonel, we have 65 ter 427.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could see that on the screen, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see a document that's popped up on the right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's the declaration presented to me and signed by me on the 17th of July, during that meeting originally meant for the coordination of the transfer of the wounded out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 427 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I take it that this is the same document now with a signature of the witness on the English version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about the same things, but this is the English translation which wasn't included in the exhibit that was uploaded into e-court previously. We just have it for some reason under a separate number. They got split up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I was told that page 2 and 3 of this document contain B/C/S text. Could you please clarify that before we receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, why don't we -- just to make everything crystal clear, let's forget about P28 for the moment. Pretend we didn't see that, and we'll just proceed through 427 and we'll see if we can clarify to the Trial Chamber what documents we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are referring to 65 ter 427?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 427, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we've, I think, explained that this is the English translation which was done by your translator on the spot; is that correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we note here, if we look at the fourth paragraph, it's one of the larger ones that lists all the various participants, just for the record and I'll tie this up in a minute, we have various individuals listed, Mr. Simic, Davidovic, Vasic. Then we see a reference to General Krstic, corps security chief, Mr. Popovic, and then we have listed here a Colonel Krstic. I just note that for the record, we'll tie that up in a second, as I said. So we've got two references to a Krstic in the English translation that was done by your interpreter; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Could we see the next page, please, and see what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And now what we see here, obviously, is something that's not in your language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see, if we look at the translation of this document, which is to the left, in that big paragraph where there are a number of names listed, we see in the B/C/S original of this declaration that we have Mr. Vasic, General Krstic, Mr. Popovic, and then Colonel Kosoric. So instead of two Krstics in the original declaration which Colonel Jankovic presented to you, we have here Colonel Kosoric identified. Do you see that, sir, in the translation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm doing my best. Yes, I see it. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. So I put it to you that what happened was, when your interpreter translated this document on the fly on the 17th of July, he simply instead of writing "Kosoric" in the English version that you signed, mistakenly repeated Krstic, and that's why we saw two Krstics in the first version that we looked at, the one that you signed. Would you accept that? Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it does make sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we are done with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think we are ready to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, including the B/C/S part.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P628.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. President, just to get back to you about the citation in the Milosevic trial, just by way of background, in that case Colonel Franken's testimony was introduced via 98 bis with cross-examination. So there was a dossier of documents that came in associated with Colonel Franken and then he was made available for cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic in that case. So if we look at transcript page 28998 to 28999, we have the Prosecutor reviewing the contents of the dossier including, it's listed here as Exhibit 594, tab 18, this document that has now been introduced as P623, Colonel Franken's comments authenticating the UNMO reports based on his experience. And again, I apologise, for exceeding the time. I appreciate the Court's indulgence with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this concludes your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It does, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn. No, before you get the floor, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a question. Witness, I believe that your testimony is extremely important, like any other, actually, but yours is extremely important. You are a member of UNPROFOR, the United Nations forces on the field when these events unfolded, the events that this Trial Chamber must rule on. You were a seasoned infantry officer, you are a colonel now, and so as far as I'm concerned, your approach as a military person is extremely important. I have three questions for you. If we -- on today's transcript page 3, line 18, you mention Colonel Jankovic who arrived on July 17th with Colonel or Major Nikolic, and when Mr. Nikolic was touring the wounded, he was touring the wounded to check who was a soldier or who was a war criminal among these wounded. I don't really understand, you're a war criminal or a soldier? How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a matter of speaking. The VRS, especially Mr. Nikolic, spoke of every ABiH soldier as a war criminal. So there for him it's a synonym. It's the same because he thought that every ABiH soldier being -- the enclave being demilitarised, there couldn't be soldiers. So everyone who took up a weapon and did anything against the VRS was, in fact, an armed civilian and, by that, a war criminal because he was not authorised to use force in the direction or towards the VRS. But for him, in his way of speaking, it is the same. We said soldiers, and he was keen on finding out all those war criminals who shot at or fought with the VRS. Is that enough an answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes. Thank you. A second small question: When the facts occurred, we have heard a number of victims here in this courtroom and they sometimes regretted that the UN forces were unable to protect the civilian population. In the transcript on page 6, line 17, and page 7, line 1, you say, and I find this extremely interesting, you say, that the military position of your observation posts was nonsense, was ridiculous. The purpose of these observation posts was just to show the presence of the UN and the flag of the UN and just to show that you were present. So I'm wondering the following: Who decided on where these observation posts should be located? Was it military people in the UN or political people? Wasn't there a way to locate these observation posts in a way that they would be seen but that, militarily wise, they could be defended because later on, after soldier van Renssen was killed, obviously there was a problem. So how can you explain this, the location of these posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before DutchBat III, being the battalion I belonged to, arrived, there were two other battalions in that area. And they, the first battalion in fact determined where the OPs, observation posts, had to come. And within the UN, what do you call that, order we had, we should deter by presence, and that is the motivation that the members of that first battalion put the OPs in these ridiculous spots. Because in that time, nobody -- there was ceasefire agreements and obviously nobody thought of the possible event that there was a war again in that area. Just for your information, we did expand the number of OPs as we came there, we made three new ones, and they were positioned in another way and dug in deeper and not on the soil, so that looked more like a defensive position than the ones we had to take over from the former battalions. Does that answer your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, I understand. Thank you. And my last question is the following. Transcript page 10, line 17 and 18. You say once again, regarding the way the UN forces operate, you say that the normal military intelligence did not work at all, that you had no information, at least you didn't have the necessary information coming from the UN as far as movement of troops is concerned, or as far as anything coming from the Serbs. Now, here is my question: Your DutchBat, the DutchBat, your battalion, I know normally that in NATO troop organisation or in all US-type armies, there's always an intelligence side, you know, G2 for the staff, and for the lower troops there's Bureau 2 or S2, that's the intelligence component to the forces. So who do you blame here? Was it because DutchBat didn't have a Bureau 2 or was it the entire UNPROFOR that did not have an intelligence component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DutchBat did not have a Bureau 2 because the organisation of the battalion was given to us, ordered by us, but my G2 officer, captain, and his sergeant major were in -- were part of the crew of the operations room. He was one of the chiefs of the operations room and he did, on my order, his normal G2 work. Problem was that within UNPROFOR we got so-called intelligence reports, but, well, I don't have them anymore, but the only one with any content otherwise than on NTR, November Tango Romeo, nothing to report, was a report that some special unit of the VRS was moving from the Croatian area in the direction of Srebrenica. When I asked then, okay, where is he, what is his -- how is he composed, it's nice that you tell me that Black Tigers or something or coming down, what are they, how big are they, what arms do they have, do you have any idea about their intention, I never got an answer. Which means, and that is what I said, there never was any information otherwise that we could see from our static positions about the strength, the components, and the weaponry of the VRS in our area. When I was back in Holland, I saw that this information was available on the very moment that it -- these events occurred. There were satellite photos of the most astonishing details, single guns of the Serbs, the positions where they were, troops of soldiers gathered in a wood, assembly areas, et cetera, et cetera. That is why I said the intelligence procedures and the intelligence within UNPROFOR did not work, or they had a reason not to give it to me, but that is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take you back to transcript page 39 and to your question put by Mr. Thayer about whether you added anything to this declaration or not. Your answer is: "I could surprise my comments to nonsense." I don't know what the word "surprise" there means in the transcript. It is incorrect. Can you just explain to me exactly what you did to this document in the context of your answer which you say, "I could surprise my comments to nonsense," which I mean you are saying your comments were nonsense and the fact that you are saying it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think surprise I -- used the word "compress" and I take it we are talking about the declaration or the agreement that was signed by me on the 7th of July, because I can't refer to what you said to me, transcript page 39 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I can explain for you a little bit. I'm particularly referring to this part: "No incidents were provoked by any side of the evacuation, and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the International Law of War." So this question is asked in the context of that addition to that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I tried to say is that I could comment every single point of the declaration but I tried to shorten it to a general comment, that what standing there, what was mentioned there or declared there was actually nonsense because it was not applicable. It was not the way the declaration says it was. And probably I use the wrong word, sorry for that. But that is why I said I could compress my comment to the word "nonsense," and that is exactly the reason why I did handwrite the sentence we spoke about. I hope I gave an answer. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: To what are you referring to as being incorrect? The sentence you added or the document to which you added the sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document, Your Honour. The content of the document was incorrect and to make that clear, that that was my position, I added that sentence. And I already thought I made clear why was what the argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, again, Mr. Tolimir, it's your turn. Please, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everyone present here, including the witness. May the Lord give peace to this courtroom, and I wish for this trial to be concluded according to the God's will and not according to what I wish. After we look at document P607, which is the statement given by witness, I would like to put a few questions to him, so could we please have that document on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see here the statement given on the 22nd and 27th September, 1995. To whom did you give this statement? Did you give it to members of the Dutch army, or did you give this statement to representatives of the International Tribunal, because there's no indication about that in this statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm just trying to read it, and seeing the fact that it was given within the military barracks in Holland, that would be probably given to the commission assigned by the Ministry of Defence after we came back to investigate the situation, or what happened in the enclave. But that is the only reason -- location where this statement was made, that is the base of my conclusion, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, because I gave that much statements that I can't recognise it from paper where I give it, but that is logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe just to save some time, if the witness can be shown page 8 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S, that just might help move things along on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you may look at the witness acknowledgement on the bottom of that page, perhaps you can identify the people you gave the statement to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that more or less confirms me my previous statement, that this statement was given to the committee that, on order of the Ministry of Defence, did survey to the way of things in the enclave when we returned, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Franken. It's clear now to whom you gave this statement. It is important for us that we see that it's authentic, that you actually did give it, and that I can ask questions on the basis of that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 in Serbian, and I'd like to keep page 1 in English. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the period while the DutchBat was deployed in Srebrenica, you were deputy battalion commander of Colonel Karremans, and you were head of the logistics as well, and all this is stated in the first paragraph of your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us, when you took over the duty, had you been briefed previously about the situation pertaining to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, during the preparation of the battalion before we went there, there was a weekly brief about the situation. And I took over on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, had you received any specific information about deployment, arms, and locations where members of the VRS were, and things of that nature? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That information I got from DutchBat II, which was the battalion was -- we were -- that was there before us. And we got some information about VRS, some brigade structures were recognised, and there was information about personnel or the liaisons with which we had to deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please supplement this answer that you have given me by telling me whether you had any information about members of the BH army, its members and the lines that they held?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct. In fact, the same sort of information we knew that the BiH had a brigade structure as well within the enclave. We more or less knew which brigade was operating in which zone, and we knew that they still had about 4.000, 4500 rifle-like weapons, mostly the Kalashnikov AK-47.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, were you surprised by the fact that you arrived in a demilitarised zone and that in spite of that, there were two parties to the conflict and that they were both armed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I was not surprised because the information I already got in Holland was that the ABiH was not completely demilitarised in the area. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, you said that they had brigades within their structures, you knew their locations, and that they had about 4.500 people armed with Kalashnikovs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, according to what you knew, what was the strength of a BH brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, they had not an organisation and not every brigade was as big as the other one. A brigade more indicated that they had some kind of an area of responsibility and they called that a brigade. I know of the units being responsible for the area around our HQ was not bigger than about 200, 300 men, but we never saw them together. It was guessing and just extracting from pieces of information we got. For instance, the brigade in the Bandera triangle, as we call it, it's the area in the southwest of the enclave, was much stronger. But how big exactly, we don't know. We didn't know, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned this triangle, there were soldiers of yours there who had been disarmed, we can deal with that later. However, what is your assessment? What was that force that took prisoner 100 of your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I was one of those soldiers. We were not disarmed and we were not taken prisoner, but probably we come to that later. Your question was, what was that force that took prisoner of 100. Well, they didn't take prisoner, but I think you mean what was the unit in the Bandera triangle. It was an area where we did not have freedom of movement. We tried to establish that on orders of Sector North-east, did not succeed, and when we tried to push on, so do that more massively, the UN withdrew his order and said, okay, leave it. In that area, there was -- at the outside it looked like a more or less organised unit, and the leader of the -- the brigade commander, who I know by the name of Zulfo, well, that's a fact the -- everything we know about it because we were not allowed to enter that area, so what exactly was this that area we did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the villages in the area that you controlled, where the population from which the BH Army had been recruited lived, did they have armed units? Were they organised on the basis of villages in terms of their army, because here we have maps and other documents relating to the Army of Republika Srpska for brigades and whatever, but now let us see what it was that you had concerning that enclave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The only thing we knew about their local organisation was the Bandera triangle unit was organised based on villages and the area around that, so they recruited the soldiers locally from those villages. How it worked in the rest of the enclave, we did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you only studied that part of the enclave where you came into conflict with them, where you encountered certain problems when carrying out your own tasks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, that does not mean that we tried to get information only about the units in the Bandera triangle. We tried to get that information from the other units as well, but on questions, we didn't get an answer. And seeing the fact that the ABiH was not uniformed in any way, it was incredibly difficult to try to identify units or the, what do you say, the number of members of a unit because, yeah, well, if we are all civilians and only they knew who was a soldier and who was not a soldier. We could not identify units. Again, they were not uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they carry rifles when they wore civilian clothing, when you say that it was hard to tell who was who because they didn't have uniforms? Did your superior command ever ask you for a report on how many armed groups were there and how they used these weapons, in shifts, two or three shifts, various positions? Because during your examination, you said that there were three lines of separation. I'm sure that you toured these lines of separation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Your first question, they did not carry rifles because the few times that we discovered them carrying rifles, we tried to unarm them. We had one small problem, the very moment they flew into a house, we were not authorised to enter that house and we had to call the local police and then have them check the house. So that was not very effective, so to say. Your second question was, my superior command never asked me details about the present ABiH which should have been logical, but awhile ago I already told that you the whole intelligence cycles didn't work within UNPROFOR. And lines of separation between the brigades, I assume you mean, no, I did not tour them because I never could find any confirmation of the fact that there was a line of separation. When there were people around, there were civilians and they never -- we never saw, until the final attack, that all the positions were taken or there was personnel in their ditches, et cetera. It was once in awhile and occasionally on different spots, so it was very difficult so if not impossible, again, to identify units and their lines of separation and their operation zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we have reached the time to have the second break, then after that you may continue your cross-examination. We adjourn now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank the witness, too. And I would now like to have a look at P107 that was tendered by the Prosecution. Could we have that in e-court. We see what the deployment of forces was there, we can see what the UNPROFOR had and what other parties had, and you could explain this to us. P107 in e-court, please. Thank you. Thank you. Could you please show in e-court the map where there were translations into both languages so that the witness could see that. Could you please display the map with the translation. Thank you. Thank you. Could you please zoom in the part where there is the text in Serbian and in English that pertains to Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There is Zepa and Srebrenica here, but we are going to look at what has to do with Srebrenica. Can you read it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can you zoom in a bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we see that it says what the population is, between 35- and 38.000. The forces of the 28th Division of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH are in the enclave. The division consists of the following brigades: The 280th, the 281st, the 282nd, the 283rd, the 284th, and the battalion of the Light Infantry Brigade. The division has about 5.000 to 5.500 troops. Police forces have 200 to 250 men. Muslim forces in Srebrenica are armed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's not necessary to read the whole text on the record because we have this as an exhibit already. Perhaps you just -- and the witness can read it. Just put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that there were five brigades there, as written here, and that the Muslim forces were armed, as is written here, and as you could read for yourself because I did not read out the whole text to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Please give me a moment to read the whole text, just hold. Yes, I read the text about the Muslim forces. As I recollect we identified four brigades, not five. The number of troops they had were, to my knowledge, 4.500, the not number standing here. The police force astonishes me. When you have a police force of about 50, 60 men, so I can't imagine where the number -- at least the number 200, 250 is strange to me. The arms that are described there, I only can confirm that we knew they had semi-automatic and automatic rifles and some light machine-guns. The hand-held rocket launchers, well, rumours about them but never saw them. The heavier weapons were, as far as I can see, all in the weapon collection point at the compounds of B Company in Srebrenica. The amount of ammunition I did not know or at least I knew not that there should have been enough. Commander Naser Oric is known to me. Then UNPROFOR, Dutch battalion did not have 550 troops to the extent within the enclave we claimed to 312. 21 APCs is correct, only the anti-tank missile systems are connected to the APCs here, that's incorrect. They were portable systems. There are currently, I don't know what currently is, 340 soldiers in the enclave, yeah, well, I don't know the date but they thought about saying 340 but that is the max, a bit less but the max we had in the enclave before. As a result of what we called convoy terror, that number was diminished. Is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Could you just tell us, for the sake of the transcript, you said there were only 500 soldiers, but a moment ago you said that there were between 4.000 and 4.500 and that there was an equal number of rifles. Is that what you said here? Is that what you actually said or did you misspeak perhaps or was this a mistranslation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I -- the number 500 was, as far as I know, not spoken by me, but I meant to say that there were about 4.500 armed men within the enclave being a member of the ABiH, as far as we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I state that in addition to the corrections that you made, you assessed all the rest as being realistic, except that you said that there were four brigades rather than five as stated here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't recognise it as a question. Yes, to my knowledge, there were only four brigades. I am sorry, Your Honour, I thought it was a statement not a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a mixture of a statement and a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you -- well, thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show in e-court what the deployment of forces was. Can you enlarge the red and blue lines so that the witness could see that. Thank you. Thank you, that's right. Could you scroll down a bit more so that we see Srebrenica rather than Zepa. Thank you. Thank you. This is what we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please indicate to us here where the Bandera triangle is because that is what we'll be dealing with in our next questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That would be approximately because to give it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: About this area, like that. And it's not adequate, but then I have to see a further in-zooming of the map, but that's the Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, while we are looking at the map, can you infer why you were blocked by the BH Army and why you were not allowed to move about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have to pick up some history. When we took over from DutchBat II, there was not a freedom of movement in that area because the local brigade commander didn't want UN to come in. That had something to do with an incident of a not -- just a temporary OP, being Bravo, in the midst of that Bandera triangle, more or less around that point. That was reported to the UN, of course, and the -- in January, when we just arrived, we got order to restore or try to restore our freedom of movement in that Bandera triangle. We made our plan and had about, let me just think, totally six patrols who were bound to enter the Bandera triangle. The first patrol that went in was led by me with the purpose of establishing a new OP in the centre of that area so we would have that under control. Doing so, I was blocked by the brigade commander and about 40 armed infantry men, my patrol was seven men, who tried to get us out of there. I did not respond and took a route generally west through the area. In the meantime, the other patrols were started and entered that area. Well, to make a long story short, we were all blocked by superior forces and we couldn't return to our base. That's when I decided to go with my patrol and a battalion reserve we met, about 3, 4 APCs who was waiting to, if necessary, help within the Bandera triangle, to retreat to OP Charlie, being an observation post to the CL directly on the south border of the Bandera triangle. And then we -- I proposed to my battalion commander to get in again and with more force. I don't know whether he had some -- some discussion with the UN or not, but that was not done, and I had to stay on my spot and wait. They were negotiating. That is the story you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell us whether this point that is marked with a black circle here, where you put a blue marking, a blue triangle, was that removed afterwards, after this protest by the Muslims? Was this UNPROFOR checkpoint moved away and could you mark that also, using the blue colour, where it was moved to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I understand your question, but I have to make something clear. If the black point is our OP Bravo, which I so to see is, OP Bravo was not always teamed, not always manned. So in the time this took place, OP Bravo was not manned; there was just the infrastructure of that OP was present. What I meant by the aim of my patrol was that directly eastly of Bravo there's a high ridge and the idea was to make a new -- to establish a new OP in that area, so you couldn't speak of removing anything. We never came to establish that new OP, and the old Bravo was not manned, so empty. Is that an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You did give an answer, but could you just mark the place where you were, because you were not in this triangle, so could you please mark the place where you were that was closest to the triangle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably a misunderstanding. I was in the triangle because I personally commanded the first patrol that went in. And I came - just hold please - around here. There I was stopped by the ABiH, as described before, and I went out in this direction, came out at this point. There we were blocked by and out-forced by the ABiH, and that's the point where I decided to withdraw to OP Charlie, which should have been here more or less. Is that clear, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, could you please put a number 1 near to the first spot you marked. And a number 2 to the second spot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. And a number 3 to the third spot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And to make it very clear, could you very shortly tell again what is indicated -- depicted with number 1 in the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1 is location of a UN observation post called Bravo, B. Not manned. Number 2 is the farthest limit that I got with my patrol, starting from thousand direction, came to 2, was blocked by ABiH, and proceeded in the direction that the arrow indicates. Number 3 is the existing and manned Observation Post Charlie, C, where I withdrew with my means and had to stay there in order of my CO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you tell us, within this blue triangle where you put numbers 1 and 2, later you were denied access because of the protests by the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was that we did not have -- we were not able to restore that freedom of movement because the order to do so was withdrawn by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was so important even for the UN to decide that you shouldn't be there and you were supposed to monitor and control the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: To prevent any misunderstandings, the UN first ordered us to restore our freedom of movement there, but then when it escalated, they withdrew the order. Important, of course, for the UN was that DutchBat had the complete control over the area, and important to the Muslims was an act that's only guessing. They didn't want us to see what they were doing there, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any strategic significance for the Muslims that they went to such length to bring this issue before the UN, and that is to say that there were discussions between your superior command, Sarajevo, Zagreb, and the UN headquarters, was that point so strategically important?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you look to defensive strategy, it is in that way important that it is one of the easier approaches within -- into the enclave, seeing the terrain there. If you should look offensively, it is not important because it's only of interest for armoured forces, and they didn't have armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the first answer, when you said that these two enclaves were close to one another, can you tell me how fast one could pass from one enclave to another?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the image back on the screen in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there happened a mistake. The markings were lost. We have to do them again, if you want to tender the marked map, Mr. Tolimir. I think it is appropriate to have it done again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely what I wanted, and I would kindly ask the witness to put the triangle again and numbers 1, 2, and 3, so that we can admit this thus marked map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please repeat that again, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. That should do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This marked map will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we still have the map on the screen, can you please draw this path that was connecting the two enclaves and you said that was very important in view of the closeness between the two enclaves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The map should be scrolled up a little bit. Yes. And now please try to mark this corridor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will as far as possible, Your Honour. The only thing I know is that there were movements of the ABiH in the direction of Zepa, but we thought to know where they go -- went out, that's one of the reasons where we build a new OP, Observation Post Delta, but what path they followed, I don't have a clue. So I can't draw that path. The fact is that Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves were relatively close. Another question of Mr. Tolimir that I -- whether I could give an indication how long it would take to go or how fast one could pass from one enclave to the other, I can't give that answer this way because I'll have to study the terrain, and I suppose that he means by foot, and that would be theoretically -- I don't have the knowledge which path and how long it took. The only thing I can see, as you can, is that both enclaves are pretty close together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we keep losing this image with the triangle, can you please use this other map and mark the entry to the enclave by using a number 4, because you knew where that was because you wanted to install your observation post so that you can know where the point of entry was for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify the situation, the marked map is not -- was not lost again, but it's an exhibit. And if you want to have an additional marking to the marked map, you should indicate that, otherwise this one should be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before it was admitted, I wanted the witness to mark the entry point to Srebrenica from Zepa which is where they wanted to install their point, and that was the reason that sparkled the conflict in which the UN was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should we have the map D65 again on the screen. There it is. Now, you could ask the witness to mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, we can see the map. Could you please just indicate with an arrow the entry point next to which you wanted to set up your point. So just put an arrow as an entry point into this zone by unauthorised persons.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, first a remark, I did not know exactly where it was. We had one report that's a column of police came in and so we concluded that that was at least one of the routes where the ABiH went out of. That's in the area of Delta. And it is -- sorry, in this area. The other one we suggested and not confirmed that was a possibility was in the area of Kilo, I suppose you want all the routes we estimated as very possible, was here. Another route there, in this area, and, yeah, well, I can't pinpoint it, is directly beneath the Bandera triangle, where you see all those brown lines, was impossible to establish an OP there because we did not have the means anymore, which meant we were not able to build anything there, infrastructure, and that had something to do with what I called convoy terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please put a 5, near the last --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, is this sufficiently marked and would you tender this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: One more thing, was there any spot within the triangle from which one can exit the zone and go to another zone, and you said that you had been driven from that point next to the road, your OP, actually, which was installed by the road was removed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to ask you a question just to make sure that I understand the question correct. You asked me to a spot in the triangle and my OP actually was installed by the road and removed. I did not understand that. What are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You understood it well. Can you please mark where this observation point, where you didn't have any people manning it, and to which you had no access any longer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't usually ask questions when I understand something, but I now understand that you meant OP Bravo and it's already marked with the figure 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, for having your marks admitted, next to number 1, can you put an X, because we have no legend in this map. Or rather mark it with a number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is marked with a number 1. At the outset, the witness indicated that this is the observation point -- Observation Post Bravo. It is not necessary to mark it again with a different letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This could have been Bravo post just like any other post, however, this one was strategically important and that was why UNPROFOR was driven away from it. That's why I'm asking the witness to put an X or any other mark indicating the place from which they had been chased out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll put an X additional to the 1. There you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later, because today we are not going to have enough time, we are going to see in Muslim documents why this was strategically important and that's why I asked you to do the markings as I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would kindly ask now for this map with all the markings inserted by the witness to be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Should that replace D65? To have all markings on one map? It will be received, and I would like to ask the Registrar to tell us the right number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The new -- the map with the new markings has now been saved as D65. Therefore, has replaced the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for clarifying this situation regarding the Bandera triangle to all of us. Now, I would kindly ask the witness to lay a foundation for something that I would like to know whether I understood properly. This was the deployment of forces 1 and 2, blue were the Muslims and the red were the Serbs. As for UNPROFOR, can you please use a pencil that you, as UN, marked as a line, and you were asked about this by the Prosecution. You can probably connect these dots, if possible. Can you please say which particular line you had in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I take it you refer to what I call the UN boundary; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, when I connect the points, being our OPs, just like this, then probably it wouldn't be very accurate because then I have to look in detail. But generally, the UN border, it's almost impossible to do that. It's 15 years ago that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this UN line coinciding with the Muslim line, the Serbs line, or was it somewhere in between? You referred to it as the Morillon line, can you indicate where it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was in general, when I can see it like this, in between those lines. It was further outside the enclave as the blue line marked on this map, and it was farther inside the enclave as the red line, the red positions marked on this map. But it's impossible for me to put a line on this map with any accuracy, and I hope you understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before this -- now the map disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you please put a dotted line indicating this imaginary line, we are not going to consider it a real one, and you can indicate in your own handwriting that it was an imaginary line stretching and running between the lines held by the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Two issues, Mr. President. The first is I think Colonel Franken has been clear that it's, and I'm just quoting from his last answer, "It's impossible for me to put a line on this map with any accuracy, and I hope you understand that." The second issue is, General Tolimir is showing Colonel Franken a map that has different coloured circles on it, as we see, these representations, and I think it's incumbent upon him to lay a foundation or at least tell Colonel Franken what his position is with respect to when this map was created, what period of time these boundaries as reflected on the map reflect, as of what time, and then ask Colonel Franken if he insists, and if the Trial Chamber insists, on Colonel Franken trying to draw this line that he has said it's impossible for him to draw. Otherwise, I don't think this is going to be very helpful to anybody if we don't have any date context or even any idea of what exactly these lines are supposed to represent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should carry on, but take into account that the witness said, "It's impossible for me to put a line on this map with any accuracy." What is the purpose to draw a line without any accuracy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, can you indicate the so-called Morillon line, because you had spoken about three lines, so in order for all of us to have a clear picture about this problem, you should do this because it was something that the Prosecutor asked you about as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can indicate, and I already indicated, that the -- let's start it another way. I take it that the blue lines on this map are more or less the defensive positions of the ABiH. And the red lines, I recognise a lot of VRS positions. Well, let's be clear about that. The so-called Morillon line is in between those lines and only, as I recollect, in the north-western part, the line went exactly between those two OPs directly, really straight, not recognisable in the area. So there you could say the blue positions are a bit out of the UN line as I see it now on this map. But then again, I take it the blue lines or more or less the positions the ABiH had prepared for defence, and I can't guarantee that they are accurately on the spot. That's impossible on this map. And I take it the red lines are VRS positions. And I already described Morillon line is in between there, these positions. So it means that positions of the ABiH are more or less within the Morillon lines, not denying the fact that they already discussed about that the Morillon line was not the correct line, but that is the actual situation I see on this map. Morillon line somewhere between the blue lines and the red line. And again, Your Honour, it's absolutely impossible to -- even if I indicated with dots, it is more or less useless because that can differ 4- or 500 metres. We are talking about a confrontation line, 400, 500 metres accuracy or lack of accuracy is deadly, is nonsense. So I hope I gave an answer and answered your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think, Mr. Tolimir, this very precise description of the recollection of this witness should be sufficient for your purposes in comparison to this map shown to the witness. We have only two or three minutes left, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Franken, for your explanation. Can you just tell me this: Was the Morillon line the line that existed in the gap that was between the red line and the blue line?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I tried to make clear in my former statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have clarified the position of that line and it will become even more clear tomorrow when we discuss other documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with this, I would like to conclude. I'm not going to raise a new topic because we only have two or three minutes, if you agree, Mr. President. And I would like to thank everyone for the assistance with my Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. I'm not sure if there was another problem with the marked map, so I would like to have D65 again on the screen. Yes, we see the cross has disappeared again. Would you please, for the second time, put a cross below the number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, there's the cross. It should be saved now, and this new marked map should replace D65 so that we have a complete picture. Thank you very much. We have reached the end of today's hearing. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning. And, sir, you have to come back tomorrow morning, and please be reminded that it is not appropriate to have contact to either party on the content of your testimony. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
